decks.title: Three Dimensional Geometry — Part 1: Direction cosines and the equation of a line
goals: Find direction cosines and direction ratios of a line
Use the fact that the squares of the direction cosines add to 1
Test points for collinearity using direction ratios
Write the vector and Cartesian equations of a line
Convert a Cartesian equation to standard form

slides.heading: Three Dimensional Geometry, Part 1
slides.body_md: Lines in space: which way they point, and how to write them down.

visual.alt: A three dimensional sketch with x, y and z axes from the origin O. A straight line passes through two marked points A and B in space; it is not parallel to any axis.
visual.caption: Two points fix a line in space (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Welcome to three dimensional geometry. In earlier classes you described points in space with three coordinates. Now we describe whole lines. A line in space is fixed by a point and a direction, or by two points. In this part you will learn to measure direction with direction cosines and ratios, and to write the equation of a line in two forms.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write the **vector** and **Cartesian** equations of a line
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part one. First, direction cosines and direction ratios. Then a key fact: the squares of the direction cosines always add up to one. Next, a quick test for three points on a line. Finally, the two forms of the equation of a line, and how to put a messy equation into standard form.

slides.heading: Direction cosines
slides.body_md: If a directed line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the positive $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes, its **direction cosines** are $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a segment from the origin O to a point P in space. The segment makes angles alpha, beta and gamma with the x, y and z axes.
visual.caption: $OP$ makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes; $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$.

slides.narration: Picture a line through the origin pointing towards a point P. It makes an angle alpha with the x axis, beta with the y axis and gamma with the z axis. The cosines of these three angles are the direction cosines of the line, usually called l, m and n. Reversing the direction of the line changes every angle to its supplement, so all three cosines change sign.

slides.heading: The key identity
slides.body_md: $l$, $m$, $n$ are the components of a **unit vector** along the line, so

visual.alt: Table of direction cosines: the x axis has 1, 0, 0; the y axis 0, 1, 0; the z axis 0, 0, 1; a line making equal angles with all three axes has plus or minus one over root 3 for each.
visual.caption: In every row the squares add up to $1$.

slides.narration: Why do the squares add up to one? Because l, m and n are the components of a unit vector along the line, and a unit vector has length one. Check the table. The x axis has direction cosines one, zero, zero. A line making equal angles with all three axes has each cosine equal to one over root three. In every case the squares add up to one.

slides.heading: Quick check: the identity
slides.body_md: Recall the key identity.
slides.narration: Try this one. Think about what kind of vector has components l, m and n.

slides.heading: Direction ratios
slides.body_md: Any three numbers $a, b, c$ **proportional** to $l, m, n$ are **direction ratios**. To get the cosines, divide by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$.

visual.alt: Table: direction ratios 2, minus 6, 3 and 4, minus 12, 6 both give direction cosines 2 over 7, minus 6 over 7, 3 over 7; reversing all signs reverses the direction cosines.
visual.caption: Many sets of ratios, one line; divide by the length to get the cosines.

slides.narration: Direction cosines are often fractions with square roots, so we also use direction ratios. These are any three numbers proportional to the cosines. Two, minus six, three is one set; four, minus twelve, six is another set for the same line. To go back to the cosines, divide each ratio by the square root of the sum of their squares, here seven. The sign depends on which way the line is directed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the third angle
slides.body_md: A line makes $120^\circ$ with the $x$-axis and $45^\circ$ with the $y$-axis. Find its angle with the $z$-axis.

visual.alt: Table for the worked example: angle 120 degrees with x has cosine minus one half, square one quarter; 45 degrees with y has cosine one over root 2, square one half; so the square of cos gamma is one quarter.
visual.caption: $\cos\gamma = \pm\dfrac12$: $\gamma = 60^\circ$ or $120^\circ$.

slides.narration: Use the identity. The cosine of one hundred and twenty degrees is minus one half, whose square is one quarter. The cosine of forty five degrees squared is one half. So the square of cos gamma is one quarter, and cos gamma is plus or minus one half. The angle is sixty or one hundred and twenty degrees, depending on the direction chosen along the line.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: through two points
slides.body_md: Find the direction ratios and direction cosines of the line from $A(2, -1, 3)$ to $B(4, 5, 0)$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with the segment from A, at 2, minus 1, 3, to B, at 4, 5, 0. The direction from A to B is given by the differences of the coordinates.
visual.caption: $\vec{AB} = 2\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, $AB = 7$.

slides.narration: For a line through two points, subtract coordinates to get direction ratios: two, six and minus three. The distance from A to B is the square root of four plus thirty six plus nine, which is seven. Divide each ratio by seven. The direction cosines are two sevenths, six sevenths and minus three sevenths. Quick check: four plus thirty six plus nine over forty nine is one.

slides.heading: Quick check: valid cosines?
slides.body_md: Which set can be direction cosines?
slides.narration: Square each number in every option and add. Only one option gives exactly one.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: collinear points
slides.body_md: Show that $P(1, 2, -1)$, $Q(3, -2, 5)$ and $R(4, -4, 8)$ are collinear.
bullets: **Step 3 —** They share $Q$, so all three points lie on one line

visual.alt: Table for the collinearity example: PQ has ratios 2, minus 4, 6; QR has 1, minus 2, 3; PR has 3, minus 6, 9. All are multiples of 1, minus 2, 3.
visual.caption: Proportional ratios and a shared point: $P$, $Q$, $R$ are collinear.

slides.narration: Three points are collinear when the segments joining them point the same way. The ratios for P Q are two, minus four, six, and for Q R one, minus two, three. The first set is twice the second, so the segments are parallel. Since they share the point Q, they lie along one straight line. Always mention the common point, or the argument is incomplete.

slides.heading: Vector equation of a line
slides.body_md: The line through the point with position vector $\vec{a}$, parallel to $\vec{b}$, is

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes. A fixed point A with position vector a, and a general point P on the line through A. The step from A to P is lambda times the direction vector b, and the position vector of P is r.
visual.caption: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$: start at $A$, move any multiple of $\vec{b}$.

slides.narration: Now the equation of a line. Start at a fixed point A with position vector a. To reach any other point P of the line, move some multiple of the direction vector b. So the position vector of P is a plus lambda b. Every real value of lambda gives a point of the line, and every point of the line comes from some lambda. Through two points, use their difference as the direction.

slides.heading: From vector to Cartesian form
slides.body_md: With $\vec{a} = x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$, compare components and eliminate $\lambda$:

nodes.label: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$
$x = x_1 + \lambda a$, $y = y_1 + \lambda b$, $z = z_1 + \lambda c$
$\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c} = \lambda$

visual.alt: Flow from the vector equation r equals a plus lambda b, to the three coordinate equations, to the Cartesian form where each fraction equals lambda.
visual.caption: Vector form to Cartesian form in two steps.

slides.narration: Write the vector equation in components. Then x equals x one plus lambda a, and similarly for y and z. Solve each for lambda and set them equal. That gives the Cartesian form: three equal fractions, with the point in the numerators and the direction ratios in the denominators. If a denominator is zero, it simply means that coordinate stays constant along the line.

slides.heading: Quick check: a point on the line
slides.body_md: Which point satisfies the equation?
slides.narration: Substitute each point and see whether all three fractions give the same value.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: point and direction
slides.body_md: Write the vector and Cartesian equations of the line through $(3, -2, 1)$ parallel to $2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table: the line through 3, minus 2, 1 parallel to 2 i plus j minus 4 k, in vector form and in Cartesian form, with the point 5, minus 1, minus 3 obtained by putting lambda equal to 1.
visual.caption: One line, two forms, and a quick point check.

slides.narration: The point gives the vector a, three i minus two j plus k. The direction is two i plus j minus four k. So the vector equation is a plus lambda times that direction. For the Cartesian form, change the signs of the point in the numerators: x minus three, y plus two, z minus one, over two, one and minus four. Always check one point.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: through two points
slides.body_md: Find the equations of the line through $A(1, 4, -2)$ and $B(3, 1, 2)$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with the segment joining A, at 1, 4, minus 2, and B, at 3, 1, 2. The line through them has direction B minus A.
visual.caption: Direction $\vec{b} - \vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$.

slides.narration: With two points, first find the direction: B minus A gives two, minus three, four. Then use A as the fixed point. The Cartesian form has x minus one, y minus four and z plus two in the numerators. Check with B. All three fractions become one, so B is on the line. Using B as the fixed point gives an equally correct equation.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: standard form first
slides.body_md: Find a point and direction ratios of $\dfrac{2x - 1}{3} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{4 - z}{5}$.

visual.alt: Table converting each fraction to standard form: 2 x minus 1 over 3 becomes x minus one half over three halves; y plus 2 over 2 stays; 4 minus z over 5 becomes z minus 4 over minus 5.
visual.caption: Point $\left(\dfrac12, -2, 4\right)$; ratios $3, 4, -10$ after doubling.

slides.narration: Before reading anything, the coefficients of x, y and z must each be one. Divide the top and bottom of the first fraction by two. Rewrite four minus z as minus of z minus four, which moves the minus sign to the denominator. Now read the point: one half, minus two, four. The ratios are three halves, two, minus five, or three, four, minus ten after doubling.

slides.heading: Quick check: parallel or the same?
slides.body_md: Decide carefully.
slides.narration: Parallel directions are not the whole story. Check whether a point of one line lies on the other.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
slides.body_md: The key ideas on one card.

rows: any numbers proportional to $l, m, n$

visual.alt: Summary table: direction cosines have squares adding to 1; direction ratios are proportional to them; a line through two points has ratios equal to the coordinate differences; the vector form is r equals a plus lambda b; the Cartesian form has three equal fractions.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up. Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles with the axes, and their squares add to one. Direction ratios are any numbers proportional to them. A line through two points has ratios equal to the coordinate differences. A line through a point parallel to a vector has vector equation a plus lambda b, and a Cartesian form with three equal fractions.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Rewrite lines in **standard form** before reading point or ratios
Direction cosines need the **square root** of the sum of squares, not the sum
Check your equation with one point

nodes.label: Rewrite in standard form: coefficient of $x$, $y$, $z$ equal to $1$
Read the point with changed signs, ratios from the denominators
Check by substituting a point
Plane questions are not in the 2026–27 syllabus

visual.alt: Exam-tip flow: first rewrite the Cartesian equation so that x, y and z have coefficient 1; then read the point with changed signs and the ratios from the denominators; then check with a point. Questions on planes are outside this year’s syllabus.
visual.caption: Most lost marks come from skipping the standard form.

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Always rewrite a Cartesian equation in standard form first. To get direction cosines, divide by the square root of the sum of squares, not by the sum. In collinearity proofs, mention the common point. Check every equation by substituting a point. Planes are not part of this year’s syllabus, so this chapter is only about lines.

decks.title: Three Dimensional Geometry — Part 2: Angles between lines and shortest distance
goals: Find the angle between two lines
Use the conditions for perpendicular and parallel lines
Decide whether two lines intersect, are parallel or are skew
Find the shortest distance between skew lines
Find the distance between parallel lines

slides.heading: Three Dimensional Geometry, Part 2
slides.body_md: When lines miss each other: angles and shortest distances.

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level, and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. In a plane, two lines either meet or are parallel. In space there is a third possibility. Two lines can pass each other without meeting and without being parallel, like a flyover above a road. Such lines are called skew. In this part you will find angles between lines, and the shortest distance between them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **shortest distance** between skew lines
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part two. Angles between lines, using only their directions. The quick tests for perpendicular and parallel lines. A method to classify any pair of lines. And two distance formulas: one for skew lines, one for parallel lines. These formulas carry five mark questions in board papers, so we will practise them step by step.

slides.heading: Angle between two lines
slides.body_md: For lines along $\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{b}_2$ (ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$), the acute angle $\theta$ satisfies

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

math: \cos\theta = \left|\dfrac{\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2}{|\vec{b}_1|\,|\vec{b}_2|}\right| = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\,\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}
slides.narration: The angle between two lines depends only on their directions, not on where the lines are. Take the dot product of the direction vectors and divide by the product of their lengths. We put a modulus around it to get the acute angle, because a line has no preferred direction. This works even for skew lines, which never meet.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: an angle
slides.body_md: Find the angle between $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{k} + \mu(\hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

visual.alt: Table for the angle example: b1 is 1, 1, 0 and b2 is 0, 1, 1, each of length root 2; their dot product is 1, so cos theta is one half and theta is 60 degrees.
visual.caption: Angle between the lines: $60^\circ$.

slides.narration: Ignore the fixed points; only the directions matter. The first direction is i plus j, the second is j plus k. Their dot product is one. Each has length root two, so the product of lengths is two. The cosine of the angle is one half, and the angle is sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Perpendicular and parallel
slides.body_md: Two special cases of the angle formula:

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

slides.narration: Two special cases come straight from the formula. If the sum of products of the direction ratios is zero, the cosine is zero and the lines are perpendicular. If the ratios are proportional, the lines are parallel, and then the cross product of the directions is the zero vector. Parallel lines might even be the same line, so check a point too.

slides.heading: Quick check: the perpendicular test
slides.body_md: Recall the condition.
slides.narration: Perpendicular means the cosine of the angle is zero. Which expression must then vanish?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: find k
slides.body_md: Find $k$ so that $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 3}{k} = \dfrac{z + 1}{3}$ and $\dfrac{x + 2}{k} = \dfrac{y}{1} = \dfrac{z - 5}{-4}$ are perpendicular.

visual.alt: Table testing values of k: the sum of products 2 k plus k minus 12 is minus 3 for k equal to 3, zero for k equal to 4, and 3 for k equal to 5. Only k equal to 4 gives perpendicular lines.
visual.caption: $3k - 12 = 0$ gives $k = 4$.

slides.narration: Read the direction ratios: two, k, three and k, one, minus four. For perpendicular lines the sum of products is zero. Two k plus k minus twelve equals zero, so three k equals twelve and k is four. The table confirms that nearby values do not work.

slides.heading: Quick check: an angle
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Compute the dot product, take its modulus, and divide by the product of lengths.

slides.heading: Three kinds of pairs in space
slides.body_md: Two distinct lines in space are **intersecting**, **parallel** or **skew**. Skew lines are not parallel and never meet; they do not lie in one plane.

nodes.label: Two lines $\vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$, $\vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$
Is $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$?
Parallel (or coincident): use the parallel-lines formula
Find $(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)$
Zero: the lines intersect
Not zero: the lines are skew

visual.alt: Decision chart: if the cross product of the directions is zero the lines are parallel or coincident; otherwise compute its dot product with a2 minus a1. Zero means the lines intersect; non-zero means they are skew.
visual.caption: Three kinds of pairs in space: parallel, intersecting, skew.

slides.narration: Here is a decision chart for any pair of lines. First test the directions. If the cross product is zero, the lines are parallel. If not, compute one more number: the cross product dotted with a two minus a one. If that is zero, the lines meet. If not, they are skew. You will meet this number again in the distance formula.

slides.heading: Picture: skew lines
slides.body_md: A line along the floor and a line across the ceiling, at right angles in direction: they never meet, and they are not parallel.

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level, and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$.

slides.narration: Think of a classroom. One line runs along the floor from front to back. Another runs across the ceiling from left to right. They point in different directions, so they are not parallel, but they never meet, because one is always above the other. The dashed segment joining them, perpendicular to both, is the shortest path between them.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the pair
slides.body_md: What are such lines called?
slides.narration: Not parallel, and never meeting. What is the special name?

slides.heading: Shortest distance between skew lines
slides.body_md: The shortest distance is the length of the common perpendicular. For $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$:

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level, and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$.

slides.narration: The cross product of the two directions is perpendicular to both lines, so it points along the common perpendicular. Project the vector joining a point of one line to a point of the other onto that direction. The length of that projection is the shortest distance. That is exactly this formula: a dot product divided by the length of the cross product, with a modulus.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: skew lines
slides.body_md: Find the shortest distance between $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = \hat{j} + 3\hat{k} + \mu(\hat{j} - \hat{k})$.

visual.alt: Table of steps for the skew-lines example: cross product minus i plus j plus k of length root 3; a2 minus a1 is minus i minus j plus 3 k; the dot product is 3; the distance is 3 over root 3, which is root 3.
visual.caption: Four steps, one number.

slides.narration: Write the four vectors first. The cross product of the directions is minus i plus j plus k, with length root three. The difference of the fixed points is minus i minus j plus three k. Their dot product is one minus one plus three, which is three. Divide by root three. The shortest distance is root three units. It is not zero, so these lines are skew.

slides.heading: Distance between parallel lines
slides.body_md: For parallel lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}$, the cross product of directions is zero, so use

visual.alt: Two parallel lines L1 and L2 in space. A on L1 and B on L2 are joined; a dashed segment from B drops perpendicular to L1, and its length d is the distance between the lines.
visual.caption: $d = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}$.

slides.narration: For parallel lines the skew formula breaks down, because the cross product of the directions is zero and we cannot divide by zero. Instead, join a point of one line to a point of the other. The distance is the height of the parallelogram formed with b, which is the length of the cross product of b with that joining vector, divided by the length of b.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: parallel lines
slides.body_md: Find the distance between $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$.

visual.alt: Table of steps for the parallel-lines example: a2 minus a1 is 2 i minus 2 j plus 2 k; its cross product with b is 2 i minus 2 k of length 2 root 2; b has length 3; so d is 2 root 2 over 3.
visual.caption: Divide by the length of $\vec{b}$, not by a cross product.

slides.narration: Both lines have direction two i minus j plus two k, so they are parallel. The joining vector is two i minus two j plus two k. Its cross product with b is two i minus two k, whose length is two root two. The length of b is three. So the distance is two root two over three units.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: do the lines meet?
slides.body_md: Show that $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ intersect.

visual.alt: Table for the intersection example: x, y and z coordinates of a general point on each line; lambda equal to 1 and mu equal to 2 give the same point 3, 2, 3 on both lines.
visual.caption: All three coordinates agree: the lines meet at $(3, 2, 3)$.

slides.narration: Write a general point of each line and equate the x and y coordinates. That gives two equations in lambda and mu, with solution lambda equals one and mu equals two. Now the deciding step: test the z coordinates. Both give three. So all three coordinates agree, and the lines meet at the point three, two, three. If the z values had differed, the lines would be skew.

slides.heading: Quick check: zero distance
slides.body_md: What does a zero shortest distance tell you?
slides.narration: The directions are not parallel, and the shortest distance is zero. What must be happening?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
slides.body_md: The tools on one card.

rows: solve two coordinate equations, test the third

visual.alt: Summary table: the angle formula, the perpendicular and parallel tests, the shortest distance formulas for skew and parallel lines, and how to test whether lines meet.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up. The angle between lines comes from the dot product of their directions, with a modulus. A zero dot product means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel. For non-parallel lines, the shortest distance formula tells you whether they meet or are skew. For parallel lines, use the cross product of b with the joining vector, divided by the length of b.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: **Check for parallel** directions before choosing a formula
Expand cross products carefully; sign slips in the $\hat{j}$ term are common
Distances are never negative: take the modulus
State the conclusion: skew, intersecting or parallel

nodes.label: Write $\vec{a}_1$, $\vec{b}_1$, $\vec{a}_2$, $\vec{b}_2$ clearly first
Check parallel before using the skew formula
Expand the cross product as a determinant, carefully
Distance is a modulus: never negative
Answer: units, and say skew / intersecting

visual.alt: Exam-tip flow: write the four vectors first; check whether the lines are parallel before choosing the formula; expand the cross product carefully; take the modulus so distance is never negative; finish with units and the kind of pair.
visual.caption: A tidy layout earns the step marks.

slides.narration: Final tips. Write the four vectors clearly before you start. Check for parallel directions first, because the skew formula fails for parallel lines. Expand cross products carefully: the middle term has a minus sign that students often forget. Take the modulus at the end, so a distance is never negative. And always write a one line conclusion.

notes.title: Three Dimensional Geometry — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Direction cosines
sections.body_md:
If a directed line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the positive $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes, its **direction cosines** are $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$. They are the components of a unit vector along the line, so $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. Reversing the direction changes the signs of all three.

Example: a line making $120^\circ$ with the $x$-axis and $45^\circ$ with the $y$-axis has $\cos^2\gamma = 1 - \dfrac14 - \dfrac12 = \dfrac14$, so $\gamma = 60^\circ$ or $120^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: $\cos\alpha$, $\cos\beta$, $\cos\gamma$ for the angles a directed line makes with the axes.
The angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ themselves, each between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes with a segment from the origin O to a point P in space. The segment makes angles alpha, beta and gamma with the x, y and z axes.
visual.caption: $OP$ makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axes; $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$.

sections.heading: 2. Direction ratios; line through two points
sections.body_md:
Numbers $a, b, c$ proportional to $l, m, n$ are **direction ratios**. Then $l = \pm\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$, and similarly for $m$, $n$ (same sign throughout).

For the line through $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$, direction ratios are $x_2 - x_1$, $y_2 - y_1$, $z_2 - z_1$; dividing by $PQ$ gives the direction cosines. Example: $A(2, -1, 3)$, $B(4, 5, 0)$: ratios $2, 6, -3$, $AB = 7$, cosines $\dfrac27, \dfrac67, -\dfrac37$.

**Collinearity:** $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear if the ratios of $AB$ and $BC$ are proportional (they share $B$).

key_terms.definition_md: Any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines; infinitely many sets for one line.

sections.heading: 3. Equation of a line in space
sections.body_md:
**Vector form.** Through the point $\vec{a}$ parallel to $\vec{b}$: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$. Through two points $\vec{a}$, $\vec{c}$: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{c} - \vec{a})$.

**Cartesian form.** Through $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ with direction ratios $a, b, c$: $\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c}$ ($= \lambda$, giving the general point $(x_1 + \lambda a, y_1 + \lambda b, z_1 + \lambda c)$).

**Standard form first:** in $\dfrac{2x - 1}{3} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{4 - z}{5}$, rewrite as $\dfrac{x - \frac12}{\frac32} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{z - 4}{-5}$: point $\left(\dfrac12, -2, 4\right)$, ratios $3, 4, -10$.

key_terms.definition_md: The real number $\lambda$; each value gives one point of the line.
Cartesian form in which $x$, $y$, $z$ each have coefficient $1$.

visual.alt: A sketch of the axes. A fixed point A with position vector a, and a general point P on the line through A. The step from A to P is lambda times the direction vector b, and the position vector of P is r.
visual.caption: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$: start at $A$, move any multiple of $\vec{b}$.

visuals.alt: Table converting each fraction to standard form: 2 x minus 1 over 3 becomes x minus one half over three halves; y plus 2 over 2 stays; 4 minus z over 5 becomes z minus 4 over minus 5.
visuals.caption: Point $\left(\dfrac12, -2, 4\right)$; ratios $3, 4, -10$ after doubling.

sections.heading: 4. Angle between two lines
sections.body_md:
The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors (taken acute):

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\,\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}$.

- **Perpendicular:** $a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0$.
- **Parallel:** $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$ (then check a point: they may coincide).

Example: directions $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ give $\cos\theta = \dfrac12$, $\theta = 60^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The acute angle between their direction vectors; defined for skew lines too.

visual.alt: Table: the cosine of the angle between two lines is the absolute value of the sum of products of direction ratios divided by the product of their lengths; a zero sum of products means perpendicular; proportional ratios mean parallel.
visual.caption: Only the directions matter for angles.

visuals.alt: Table testing values of k: the sum of products 2 k plus k minus 12 is minus 3 for k equal to 3, zero for k equal to 4, and 3 for k equal to 5. Only k equal to 4 gives perpendicular lines.
visuals.caption: $3k - 12 = 0$ gives $k = 4$.

sections.heading: 5. Intersecting, parallel and skew lines
sections.body_md:
Two distinct lines in space are **parallel**, **intersecting** or **skew** (neither parallel nor intersecting; not coplanar).

**Do they meet?** Write general points of both lines, equate two coordinates, solve for $\lambda$ and $\mu$, and test the third coordinate. Example: $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ give $\lambda = 1$, $\mu = 2$ and the common point $(3, 2, 3)$.

**Quick test:** for non-parallel lines, $(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = 0$ exactly when they intersect.

key_terms.definition_md: Lines in space that are not parallel and do not intersect.
Lines lying in one plane (parallel or intersecting).

nodes.label: Two lines $\vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$, $\vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$
Is $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$?
Parallel (or coincident): use the parallel-lines formula
Find $(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)$
Zero: the lines intersect
Not zero: the lines are skew

visual.alt: Decision chart: if the cross product of the directions is zero the lines are parallel or coincident; otherwise compute its dot product with a2 minus a1. Zero means the lines intersect; non-zero means they are skew.
visual.caption: Three kinds of pairs in space: parallel, intersecting, skew.

visuals.alt: Table for the intersection example: x, y and z coordinates of a general point on each line; lambda equal to 1 and mu equal to 2 give the same point 3, 2, 3 on both lines.
visuals.caption: All three coordinates agree: the lines meet at $(3, 2, 3)$.

sections.heading: 6. Shortest distance between skew lines
sections.body_md:
The **shortest distance** is the length of the segment perpendicular to both lines (the common perpendicular). For $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$:

$d = \left|\dfrac{(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}\right|$.

Example: $\vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$, $\vec{b}_1 = \hat{i} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 = \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}_2 = \hat{j} - \hat{k}$: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, dot product $3$, $d = \sqrt3$.

In Cartesian form, read $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ from the standard form first. *The scalar triple product notation and planes are not in the 2026–27 syllabus; write the dot and cross products out.*

key_terms.definition_md: The segment perpendicular to both skew lines; its length is the shortest distance.

visual.alt: Two skew lines: L1 runs parallel to the x axis at floor level, and L2 runs parallel to the y axis at height 3, above it. They never meet and are not parallel. A dashed segment MN, perpendicular to both, joins them; its length is the shortest distance.
visual.caption: Skew lines and their common perpendicular $MN$.

visuals.alt: Table of steps for the skew-lines example: cross product minus i plus j plus k of length root 3; a2 minus a1 is minus i minus j plus 3 k; the dot product is 3; the distance is 3 over root 3, which is root 3.
visuals.caption: Four steps, one number.

sections.heading: 7. Distance between parallel lines; foot of a perpendicular
sections.body_md:
For parallel lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}$: $d = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}$. Example: $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ give $d = \dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.

**Foot of the perpendicular from a point $P$ to a line:** take the general point $F$ of the line, set $\vec{PF} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$, solve for $\lambda$. Example: $P(5, 3, -2)$ and $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$ give $\lambda = 2$, $F(3, 4, -2)$, distance $\sqrt5$.

key_terms.definition_md: The point of a line closest to a given point.

visual.alt: Two parallel lines L1 and L2 in space. A on L1 and B on L2 are joined; a dashed segment from B drops perpendicular to L1, and its length d is the distance between the lines.
visual.caption: $d = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}$.

visuals.alt: Table of steps for the parallel-lines example: a2 minus a1 is 2 i minus 2 j plus 2 k; its cross product with b is 2 i minus 2 k of length 2 root 2; b has length 3; so d is 2 root 2 over 3.
visuals.caption: Divide by the length of $\vec{b}$, not by a cross product.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Direction cosines (1–2 marks):* ratios from differences, the length, then each ratio divided by it.
- *Equation of a line (2–3 marks):* point and direction identified, vector form, Cartesian form.
- *Angle / perpendicular / parallel (2–3 marks):* both sets of ratios from the standard form, formula, conclusion.
- *Shortest distance (3–5 marks):* $\vec{a}_1, \vec{b}_1, \vec{a}_2, \vec{b}_2$ written, cross product, its length, dot product, final distance with units and the conclusion (skew / intersecting).

**Common mistakes**
1. Reading ratios from a line not in standard form (e.g. $\dfrac{4 - z}{5}$ has ratio $-5$).
2. Dividing direction ratios by their sum instead of by the square root of the sum of squares.
3. Forgetting the minus sign in the $\hat{j}$ component of a cross product.
4. Using the skew-lines formula for parallel lines (division by zero).
5. Forgetting the modulus, giving a negative distance or an obtuse angle.
6. Collinearity proofs without naming the common point.
7. Concluding "parallel and distinct" without checking whether a point of one line lies on the other.
8. Bringing in planes: the plane is not in the 2026–27 syllabus.

questions.stem_md: If $l$, $m$, $n$ are the direction cosines of a line, then $l^2 + m^2 + n^2$ equals
questions.solution_md: $l$, $m$, $n$ are the components of a unit vector along the line, so the sum of their squares is $1$.

questions.stem_md: The direction cosines of the $y$-axis are
questions.solution_md: The $y$-axis makes angles $90^\circ$, $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$ with the axes; their cosines are $0, 1, 0$.

questions.stem_md: Direction ratios of the line joining $P(2, 3, -1)$ and $Q(5, -1, 1)$ are
questions.solution_md: Subtract coordinates: $5 - 2 = 3$, $-1 - 3 = -4$, $1 - (-1) = 2$. Option (d) adds the coordinates; (a) and (b) have sign slips.

questions.stem_md: A line has direction ratios $2, -6, 3$. Its direction cosines are
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{2^2 + (-6)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{49} = 7$; divide each ratio by $7$ (the other choice is all signs reversed). Option (a) divides by the sum $2 + 6 + 3$.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following can be the direction cosines of a line?
questions.solution_md: Only (a) has squares adding to $1$: $\dfrac19 + \dfrac49 + \dfrac49 = 1$. The others give $\dfrac34$, $\dfrac54$ and $2$.

questions.stem_md: A line makes angles $90^\circ$, $135^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ with the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes. Its direction cosines are
questions.solution_md: $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, $\cos 135^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Check: $0 + \dfrac12 + \dfrac12 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The Cartesian equation of the line through $(1, -2, 4)$ parallel to the vector $3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: Point $(x_1, y_1, z_1) = (1, -2, 4)$ goes in the numerators with changed signs; the direction ratios $3, -1, 2$ go in the denominators. Option (d) uses the wrong signs in the numerators and (a) swaps point and direction.

questions.stem_md: Which point lies on the line $\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-2} = \dfrac{z - 5}{4}$?
questions.solution_md: Each fraction must give the same value $\lambda$. For $(5, -3, 9)$: $\dfrac33 = \dfrac{-2}{-2} = \dfrac44 = 1$. For $(5, -3, 1)$ the last fraction is $-1$. $(3, -2, 4)$ are the direction ratios, not a point.

questions.stem_md: Direction ratios of the line $\dfrac{4 - x}{2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{5} = \dfrac{2z - 1}{6}$ are
questions.solution_md: Write it in standard form: $\dfrac{x - 4}{-2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{5} = \dfrac{z - \frac12}{3}$. The ratios are $-2, 5, 3$. Option (d) reads the denominators without making the coefficients of $x$ and $z$ equal to $1$.

questions.stem_md: The vector equation of the line through $A(2, 0, -1)$ and $B(3, 2, 1)$ is
questions.solution_md: Use $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{b} - \vec{a})$: the direction is $B - A = (1, 2, 2)$. Options (c) and (a) use a position vector as the direction, and (d) adds them.

questions.stem_md: Two lines with direction ratios $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$ are perpendicular if and only if
questions.solution_md: Perpendicular means $\cos\theta = 0$, i.e. the dot product of the direction vectors is $0$. Option (d) is the condition for parallel lines.

questions.stem_md: The acute angle between two lines with direction ratios $1, -1, 0$ and $0, 1, -1$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|0 - 1 + 0|}{\sqrt2\,\sqrt2} = \dfrac12$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: For what value of $p$ are the lines $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y}{p} = \dfrac{z + 3}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x + 4}{3} = \dfrac{y - 2}{-2} = \dfrac{z}{4}$ perpendicular?
questions.solution_md: $2(3) + p(-2) + 1(4) = 0 \Rightarrow 10 - 2p = 0 \Rightarrow p = 5$.

questions.stem_md: Lines with direction ratios $2, -3, 6$ and $4, k, 12$ are parallel when $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: Parallel lines have proportional ratios: $\dfrac42 = \dfrac{k}{-3} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$, so $k = -6$.

questions.stem_md: Two lines in space that are neither parallel nor intersecting are called
questions.solution_md: Such lines do not lie in one plane; they are skew. Perpendicular lines may intersect or be skew, so (b) is not the name of this case.

questions.stem_md: For lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu\vec{b}_2$, suppose $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$ and $(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = 0$. Then the lines
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 \ne \vec{0}$ rules out parallel (and coincident) lines; a zero shortest distance then means they meet.

questions.stem_md: The shortest distance between the $x$-axis and the line $\vec{r} = 3\hat{k} + \mu\hat{j}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$ and $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 3\hat{k}$, so $d = \dfrac{|3|}{1} = 3$. The second line runs parallel to the $y$-axis at height $3$.

questions.stem_md: The distance between the parallel lines $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \lambda(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} - \hat{k}$; $\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ of length $\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt2$; divide by $|\vec{b}| = 3$: $d = \sqrt2$. Option (c) forgets to divide.

questions.stem_md: The $z$-axis has $0, 0, 1$ as its direction cosines.
questions.solution_md: The $z$-axis makes angles $90^\circ, 90^\circ, 0^\circ$ with the axes.

questions.stem_md: If $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of a line, then $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$.
questions.solution_md: That holds for direction **cosines** only. For example $2, -6, 3$ are direction ratios with squares adding to $49$.

questions.stem_md: The lines $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 3}{4}$ and $\dfrac{x - 3}{4} = \dfrac{y - 5}{6} = \dfrac{z - 7}{8}$ are parallel and distinct.
questions.solution_md: The ratios $4, 6, 8$ are twice $2, 3, 4$, so the lines are parallel. But $(3, 5, 7)$ satisfies the first equation (each fraction is $1$), so they share a point: the lines coincide.

questions.stem_md: The acute angle between lines with direction ratios $1, 1, 0$ and $-1, 0, 1$ is $60^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|-1 + 0 + 0|}{\sqrt2\,\sqrt2} = \dfrac12$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$. The modulus gives the acute angle.

questions.stem_md: Two lines in space that do not intersect must be parallel.
questions.solution_md: False: skew lines neither meet nor are parallel, e.g. the $x$-axis and the line $\vec{r} = \hat{k} + \mu\hat{j}$.

questions.stem_md: If a line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the coordinate axes, then $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = $ ____.
questions.solution_md: These are the squares of the direction cosines, whose sum is $1$.

questions.stem_md: For any line in space, the sum of the squares of the **sines** of its three direction angles is ____.
A point of the line $\dfrac{x + 3}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{-4} = \dfrac{z - 2}{5}$ has $x$-coordinate $-1$. Its $z$-coordinate is ____.
Lines with direction ratios $k, 2, -1$ and $3, k, 4$ are perpendicular when $k = $ ____.
The shortest distance between the lines $\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{i}$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{j} + \mu\hat{k}$ is ____ units.
questions.solution_md: $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$ and $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = 2\hat{j}$; $d = \dfrac{|-2|}{1}$.

questions.stem_md:
Consider the lines $L_1: \dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{2} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ and $L_2: \dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{-2} = \dfrac{z + 3}{1}$.

(a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are perpendicular.

(b) Find the shortest distance between them, and state whether they intersect.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\vec{b}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}_2 = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$; $\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2 = 2 - 4 + 2 = 0$, so the lines are perpendicular.

(b) $\vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$, $\vec{a}_2 = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, so $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = (2 \cdot 1 - 2(-2))\hat{i} - (1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2)\hat{j} + (1(-2) - 2 \cdot 2)\hat{k} = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, with $|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 36} = 9$. $(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) = 6 + 6 + 18 = 30$. $d = \dfrac{30}{9} = \dfrac{10}{3}$ units. Since $d \ne 0$, the lines do not intersect: they are skew (and perpendicular).

questions.solution_md: Dot product for (a); shortest-distance formula for (b).

questions.stem_md: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the line through $(2, -3, 1)$ that is perpendicular to both the lines $\dfrac{x + 1}{1} = \dfrac{y - 4}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 5}{1}$. Verify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the required direction ratios be $a, b, c$. Perpendicular to both: $a + 2b + 3c = 0$ and $2a - b + c = 0$. Doubling the second and adding to the first: $5a + 5c = 0$, so $c = -a$; then $b = 2a + c = a$. So $a : b : c = 1 : 1 : -1$ (the same as $\vec{u} \times \vec{v} = 5\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$).
Vector equation: $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k})$.
Cartesian: $\dfrac{x - 2}{1} = \dfrac{y + 3}{1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{-1}$.
Verify: $1 + 2 - 3 = 0$ and $2 - 1 - 1 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Two perpendicularity conditions, solved for the ratios.

answer.model_answer_md:
A common point needs $2\lambda = 1 + \mu$, $-1 + \lambda = 4 - \mu$ and $3 - 2\lambda = 2 - \mu$. Adding the first two: $3\lambda - 1 = 5$, so $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = 3$. Third equation: $3 - 4 = -1$ and $2 - 3 = -1$ ✓. So the lines intersect at $(4, 1, -1)$.
(Check by the formula: $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = -3\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1 = \hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ give $-3 + 0 + 3 = 0$.)
Angle: $\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2 = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3$, $|\vec{b}_1| = 3$, $|\vec{b}_2| = \sqrt3$, so $\cos\theta = \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.passage_md: A ropeway near Gangtok has its lower station at the origin $O(0, 0, 0)$ and its upper station at $B(300, 400, 1200)$, in metres, with the $z$-axis vertical. The cable is taken to be the straight segment $OB$.

children.stem_md: The direction cosines of the cable (from O to B) are
children.solution_md: Divide $300, 400, 1200$ by $1300$. Option (a) divides by the sum $3 + 4 + 12$; option (b) gives direction ratios only.

children.stem_md: Find the length of the cable, in metres.
**(i)** Write the vector equation of the cable line and find the position of a cabin that has travelled 650 m from O along the cable.

answer.model_answer_md: Direction ratios $3, 4, 12$: $\vec{r} = \lambda(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k})$. Moving $650$ m along the unit vector: $650\left(\dfrac{3}{13}, \dfrac{4}{13}, \dfrac{12}{13}\right) = (150, 200, 600)$.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Write the Cartesian equation of the cable line and check whether the top of a support pylon at (180, 240, 720) lies on it.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{y}{4} = \dfrac{z}{12}$. At $(180, 240, 720)$: $\dfrac{180}{3} = \dfrac{240}{4} = \dfrac{720}{12} = 60$, all equal, so the pylon top lies on the cable line.

alternatives.solution_md: Equal ratios mean the point is on the line.

marking_scheme.step: All three ratios 60 ⇒ on the line

questions.passage_md: During a drone light show in Ahmedabad, two drones fly along straight paths (units: metres). Drone P follows $\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k} + t(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ and drone Q follows $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} + s(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$. The organisers must know whether the paths cross.

children.stem_md: Which point lies on drone P's path?
children.solution_md: $t = 1$: $(1 + 2, 2 - 1, 3 + 2) = (3, 1, 5)$. $(2, -1, 2)$ is the direction, not a point of the path.

children.stem_md: If $\theta$ is the angle between the two paths, find the value of $27\cos^2\theta$.
**(i)** Show that the two paths intersect, and find the point where they cross.

answer.model_answer_md: Equate: $1 + 2t = 2 + s$, $2 - t = 3 - s$, $3 + 2t = 4 + s$. Adding the first two: $3 + t = 5$, so $t = 2$ and $s = 3$. Third: $3 + 4 = 7$ and $4 + 3 = 7$ ✓. The paths cross at $(5, 0, 7)$.

children.solution_md: Two equations give t and s; the third must agree.

marking_scheme.step: t = 2, s = 3 with the third checked

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** A third drone R flies along $\vec{r} = t(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$, parallel to the path of P. Find the distance between the paths of P and R.

answer.model_answer_md: $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$; $\vec{a}_R - \vec{a}_P = -\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. $\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_R - \vec{a}_P) = 7\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$, length $\sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}$. Distance $= \dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{3} = \sqrt{10}$ m.

questions.passage_md: In a physics lab in Pune, a laser beam leaves a source at $S(1, 1, 0)$ in the direction $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ (units: decimetres, $z$-axis up). A light sensor is fixed at $T(5, 4, 4)$, off the beam.

children.stem_md: The Cartesian equation of the beam is
children.solution_md: Point (1, 1, 0) in the numerators, direction ratios 1, 2, 2 in the denominators.

children.stem_md: Find the x-coordinate of the point where the beam is at height z = 6.
**(i)** Find the point of the beam closest to the sensor and the distance of the sensor from the beam.

answer.model_answer_md: General point $F(1 + \lambda, 1 + 2\lambda, 2\lambda)$; $\vec{TF} = (\lambda - 4)\hat{i} + (2\lambda - 3)\hat{j} + (2\lambda - 4)\hat{k}$. $\vec{TF} \cdot (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = 9\lambda - 18 = 0$, so $\lambda = 2$ and $F(3, 5, 4)$. $TF = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 0} = \sqrt5$ dm.

children.solution_md: Foot of the perpendicular from T to the beam.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** A second beam from the same source has direction 2i − 2j + k. Find the angle between the two beams.

answer.model_answer_md: $(1)(2) + (2)(-2) + (2)(1) = 2 - 4 + 2 = 0$, so $\cos\theta = 0$ and the beams are at $90^\circ$.
